title: ER Model
summary: Draw your data before you build it — the ER model turns real-world things and their connections into a blueprint for tables.

blocks.markdown:
The **ER (Entity-Relationship) model** is a design tool — you sketch real-world objects and their connections before writing a single table.

- Created by Peter Chen in 1976.
- Output is an **ER diagram** that becomes the blueprint for a relational database.
- You build it from three ideas: **entities**, **attributes**, and **relationships**.

See also [data-models](data-models) for where ER fits in the bigger picture.

blocks.subTitle: Strong vs weak
blocks.markdown:
An **entity** is a real-world object or concept worth tracking.

- **Strong entity** — has its own unique identity (e.g. Employee, Product).
- **Weak entity** — depends on another entity to be identified (e.g. Dependent depends on Employee). It can't exist alone.

A **weak entity** is always associated with its **owner entity** via an **identifying relationship**.

blocks.subTitle: Types of attributes
blocks.markdown:
An **attribute** is a property of an entity or relationship.

- **Simple** — atomic, can't be split (e.g. Age).
- **Composite** — made of parts (e.g. Name → First + Last).
- **Derived** — computed from another attribute (e.g. Age from BirthDate).
- **Multivalued** — can hold many values (e.g. PhoneNumbers).
- **Key attribute** — uniquely identifies an entity (e.g. EmployeeID).

blocks.subTitle: Attribute quick-ref
blocks.markdown:
A quick map of attribute types.

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Simple | Not splittable | Age |
| Composite | Has sub-parts | Name |
| Derived | Computed | Age from DOB |
| Multivalued | Many values | PhoneNumbers |

blocks.subTitle: What a relationship is
blocks.markdown:
A **relationship** connects two or more entities and describes how they interact.

- Example: Employee **Works_For** Department.
- Relationships can also have their own attributes — e.g. the **HireDate** of an employee–department link.
- The number of entities in a relationship is its **degree**.

blocks.subTitle: Degree (unary / binary / ternary)
blocks.markdown:
**Degree** = how many entity types participate.

- **Unary (1)** — an entity relates to itself. E.g. Employee **supervises** Employee.
- **Binary (2)** — two entity types. Most common. E.g. Student **enrolls in** Course.
- **Ternary (3)** — three entity types. E.g. Doctor **prescribes** Drug **to** Patient.

Binary relationships cover the vast majority of real designs.

blocks.subTitle: The three ratios
blocks.markdown:
**Cardinality** says how many instances of one entity can relate to instances of another.

- **1:1** — one entity on each side. E.g. Person has one Passport.
- **1:N** — one on the left, many on the right. E.g. Department has many Employees.
- **M:N** — many on both sides. E.g. Students enroll in many Courses; a Course has many Students.

blocks.subTitle: Cardinality quick-ref
blocks.markdown:
Cardinality at a glance.

| Ratio | One side | Other side |
|---|---|---|
| 1:1 | One | One |
| 1:N | One | Many |
| M:N | Many | Many |

blocks.subTitle: Total vs partial
blocks.markdown:
**Participation** says whether every entity instance must join a relationship.

- **Total (mandatory)** — every instance must participate. E.g. every Employee *must* work in a Department. Shown as a double line.
- **Partial (optional)** — some instances may not participate. E.g. not every Employee manages a project. Shown as a single line.

**Keys** uniquely identify entity instances.

- **Key attribute** — an attribute whose value is unique for every instance (e.g. EmployeeID). Underlined in ER diagrams.
- **Partial key** — a weak entity's key, unique only within its owner's group (e.g. DependentName unique per Employee). Shown with a dashed underline.

See [relational-model-keys](relational-model-keys) for how keys translate to tables.

blocks.subTitle: Shapes and symbols
blocks.markdown:
Standard Chen notation uses shapes for each element.

- **Rectangle** — strong entity.
- **Double rectangle** — weak entity.
- **Ellipse** — attribute; **double ellipse** = multivalued; **dashed ellipse** = derived.
- **Diamond** — relationship; **double diamond** = identifying relationship (for weak entity).
- **Underline** — key attribute; dashed underline = partial key.
- Lines connect entities to relationships; double line = total participation.

Common ER modeling mistakes:

- **Treating derived attributes as stored** — Age doesn't need its own column if BirthDate is stored; compute it.
- **Forgetting participation constraints** — leaving them out loses "mandatory" rules that enforce data integrity.
- **Making everything a strong entity** — weak entities exist for a reason; forcing a surrogate key on every table adds noise.
- **Confusing cardinality and participation** — cardinality is *how many*; participation is *must it*. They're orthogonal.

blocks.subTitle: Strong vs weak entity
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a weak entity and when do you use one?**

A **weak entity** has no key of its own and depends on an owner entity to be identified. Use it when an object only makes sense in the context of another — e.g. a bank account's Transaction only exists for that account. A partial key distinguishes instances within the same owner.

blocks.subTitle: Cardinality vs participation
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between cardinality and participation?**

**Cardinality** (1:1, 1:N, M:N) counts *how many* instances on each side can be connected. **Participation** (total vs partial) says *whether* every instance must be involved. For example, a Department–Employee relationship can be 1:N (cardinality) and Employee must belong to a department (total participation on the Employee side).

blocks.subTitle: Types of attributes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Name the types of attributes in the ER model.**

Simple (atomic), composite (has parts), derived (computed from another), multivalued (multiple values), and key (uniquely identifies). A real-world example combining these: a person's Name is composite, Age is derived, PhoneNumbers are multivalued, and SSN is the key.

blocks.subTitle: ER to relational
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you convert an ER diagram to a relational schema?**

Each strong entity becomes a table; its key attribute becomes the primary key. Weak entities get a table that includes the owner's primary key plus the partial key as a composite PK. M:N relationships become a separate table with both entities' keys. 1:N relationships are handled by placing the "1 side" key as a foreign key on the "N side" table. See [database-design](database-design) for full mapping rules.

blocks.subTitle: Degree of a relationship
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the degree of a relationship, and what types exist?**

Degree is the number of entity types involved. Unary (1) — an entity relates to itself, like an Employee supervising another Employee. Binary (2) — the most common, two entities. Ternary (3) — three entities, like Doctor prescribing a Drug to a Patient. Degrees higher than 3 are rare in practice.

blocks.subTitle: ER model vs ER diagram
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between the ER model and an ER diagram?**

The **ER model** is the conceptual framework — the rules for describing entities, attributes, and relationships. An **ER diagram** is a specific visual drawing of one database's design using those rules. Think of the model as the language and the diagram as a sentence written in it.
